back.body: You · your crew · the patient · bystanders — in that order, every time · An injured EMT becomes a second patient and consumes the resources sent for the first · If you cannot make it safe, STAGE and wait for who can · Size-up is continuous, not an arrival step · Scenes change while you are kneeling on them
back.why_it_matters: The instinct is to run toward the patient. Every rule here exists to override that instinct.

front.title: Standard precautions
front.summary: Dress for the task, not the diagnosis

back.body: Decided during size-up, BEFORE contact · Gloves every patient, always · Eye protection wherever splash or spray is possible: suctioning, vomiting, major bleeding, childbirth · Mask for cough or fever, and mask the patient too · Gown for heavy contamination · Upgrade as the call reveals itself
back.why_it_matters: You almost never know what a patient has. You do know what you are about to do with your hands.

back.body: Nature of illness = why a medical patient called; found by ASKING; drives a history-led focused exam · Mechanism of injury = the forces acting on a trauma patient; found by LOOKING; drives an exam aimed where the energy went · Many patients are both · Never let the visible injury hide the medical cause that produced it
back.why_it_matters: The crash is the consequence. Always ask what caused it.

front.title: Nature of illness vs. mechanism of injury
front.summary: How you find it, what it drives

back.body: Nature of illness is a medical problem found mostly by asking, and it drives a focused exam led by the history. Mechanism of injury is the physical forces found mostly by looking at the scene, and it drives an exam aimed where the energy went. A patient can have both, and the medical cause behind a crash is the one that gets missed.
back.why_it_matters: Which camp the patient is in decides the shape of everything that follows.

back.body: Count BEFORE committing to anyone · Include those who walked away, are still in a vehicle, or are not complaining · More patients than your crew can manage = MCI, switch to triage · Ask for resources EARLY — cancelling takes seconds, summoning takes minutes · Resources include police, fire, power, rescue and air medical
back.why_it_matters: The loudest patient takes all your attention, which is exactly why you count first.

back.body: Falls from height · Ejection · Death of another occupant · Rollover · High-speed collision · Penetrating injury to head, neck, chest or abdomen · Pedestrian or cyclist struck · Children and older adults are injured by far less · Drives a RAPID FULL-BODY SCAN, not a focused exam · A well-looking patient does NOT cancel it
back.why_it_matters: Mechanism raises suspicion, and suspicion is not something the patient can talk you out of.

front.title: General impression
front.summary: Sick or not sick, from the doorway

back.body: Formed in the first seconds, BEFORE you touch anyone · Built from appearance · work of breathing · skin colour · Answers one question: sick or not sick · Sets the PACE of everything that follows, not the diagnosis · A bad impression justifies calling for help before you have any numbers · Vitals lag; appearance does not
back.why_it_matters: If someone looks terrible and the numbers look fine, believe your eyes.

front.title: Level of consciousness
front.summary: AVPU, and which way they are moving

back.body: Alert · responds to Verbal · responds to Painful · Unresponsive · Alert is qualified by orientation to person, place, time, event — awake is not the same as orientated · Work DOWN the scale: look, then speak, then cause pain · GCS scores eye, verbal and motor separately and is more than the primary survey needs · The TREND beats the value
back.why_it_matters: A patient who was alert and now answers only to voice is deteriorating, whatever the letter says.

back.body: A — Alert, eyes open and interacting (qualify with orientation to person, place, time, event). V — responds to Verbal. P — responds to Painful stimulus only. U — Unresponsive to anything.
back.why_it_matters: Which rung matters less than which way they are climbing.

front.title: Airway in the primary survey
front.summary: Open now, and will it stay open?

back.body: Clear speech in full sentences = patent RIGHT NOW · Snoring = tongue · Gurgling = fluid, suction · Stridor = upper airway narrowing · SILENCE with visible effort = worst finding, nothing moving · Then ask: falling LOC, swelling, blood, vomiting? · Fix what you find HERE before moving on
back.why_it_matters: Two questions, not one. Patent now is not the same as staying patent.

back.body: Rate + depth + effort, together · Rate alone misleads — 30 shallow can move less air than 12 deep · Effort: accessory muscles, retractions, nasal flaring, few words at a time · AGONAL GASPS ARE NOT BREATHING — cardiac arrest until proven otherwise · Inadequate breathing gets ventilated HERE
back.why_it_matters: Plenty of dying patients are breathing. The question is whether it is adequate.

back.body: Pulse: carotid if unresponsive, radial if responsive · Control major external bleeding IMMEDIATELY · Skin: Colour, Temperature, Condition · Pink, warm, dry = good · Pale, cool, clammy = body shunting blood to protect the core = compensated shock · Skin changes BEFORE blood pressure does
back.why_it_matters: Blood pressure is a late sign. The skin is the cheapest monitor you own.

front.title: CTC
front.summary: What the skin is telling you

back.body: C — Colour: pink, pale, flushed, cyanotic, mottled, jaundiced. T — Temperature: warm, cool, cold, hot. C — Condition: dry, moist, clammy, diaphoretic.
back.why_it_matters: Three findings you can get with the back of one hand, faster than you can find a cuff.

front.title: Transport priority
front.summary: The survey ends in a decision

back.body: Not a summary — a decision: now, or not now · HIGH PRIORITY: bad general impression, threatened airway, inadequate breathing, uncontrolled bleeding, shock, altered or FALLING level of consciousness, severe pain · High priority = load and assess on the move · Revisable both ways — the missed one is the upgrade
back.why_it_matters: Everything done on scene is time the patient is not where they can be fixed.

front.title: XABC
front.summary: When blood is the fastest clock

back.body: ABC ranks threats by how fast they kill · X = eXsanguinating haemorrhage, placed BEFORE airway · Only for obvious catastrophic external bleeding: arterial limb bleed, amputation · In practice: tourniquet or hard pressure in seconds, then straight into airway as normal · Reorders ABC for that patient; does not replace it for everyone
back.why_it_matters: For a patient bleeding at arterial speed, blood runs down the clock faster than the airway does.
